findings.statement: Section 9.2 writes and reads the fast-path response at idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, which has no merchant_id and no request-hash comparison. This breaks principle P3, which scopes idempotency to (merchant, key). Section 9.1 also accepts merchants' own order and invoice numbers as keys, so collisions across merchants are likely. Merchant A could receive merchant B's stored payment response, and its own payment would never be created. A reused key with a different body would get the old response instead of the HTTP 422 that FR-5 requires. That means cross-merchant data disclosure plus silent loss of payments.

Section 13.1 has the Fraud Hook detokenise the full card number, using the Card Adapter's library and service role, and send it to FRV-1. Several other parts of the design contradict this: principle P2 (PAN only leaves the Vault over the Card Adapter's acquirer connection), Section 12.1 (only the Card Adapter's identity may detokenise), and Section 12.2 (Fraud Hook out of scope, token and BIN only). Sharing the role also defeats P9 least privilege. As written, the Fraud Hook and probably the Orchestrator path come into the CDE, so the NFR-5 scope cannot be assessed as defined. The FRV-1 data-processing agreement is still pending (Backlog item 4).

Section 12.4 stores the CVC encrypted until settlement or for up to 72 hours. It also re-uses it for cascades and for incremental authorizations, which happen after the first authorization. The design says PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow sensitive authentication data to be kept until settlement. The usual reading of the standard is that SAD may not be kept after authorization completes, and the requirements cited appear to cover storage before authorization, not after. If that reading is right, NFR-6 itself rests on a wrong premise, NFR-5 (Level 1 Report on Compliance) cannot be achieved, and the incremental-authorization use case is unlawful under the standard as built. No external source was available here to confirm the clause wording, so it must be checked before the Vault is built.

NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings, including when a whole region is lost. Section 20.2 replicates asynchronously with lag usually under a second, so postings committed in that window are lost. DynamoDB, Redis and MSK are rebuilt empty, so idempotency state for requests still in flight cannot be fully rebuilt. Merchant retries after failover can then produce duplicate authorizations, which breaks FR-5. The NFR-4 game day only checks postings committed before the failure, which does not exercise the loss window.

Section 12.1 unwraps every DEK in the HSM with no caching, and Section 12.3 runs one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. Losing that AZ or that HSM therefore stops all card payments. Mapping the resulting 503 to retryable does not help, because every cascade candidate goes through the same Vault. Cards are about 55% of attempts, against a 99.95% target (about 22 minutes a month) in NFR-3. The trigger for adding a second HSM (sustained card volume over 1,500 TPS) would never fire, because peak card volume is about 1,100 TPS. This challenges the approved 'one HSM at launch' decision, based on the three document items cited.

Section 21.1 keeps cascades out of the p99 by claiming fewer than 1% of card payments cascade. Section 10.5 reports 3.8% retryable outcomes, and every one of them triggers a cascade under Section 11.2. Timeout-triggered cascades alone take more than 2,500 ms, which is over the 1,500 ms NFR-2 target. NFR-2 explicitly includes cascades, and the NFR-2 test injects 3.8% retryable outcomes, so the design as written is likely to fail its own acceptance test.

The batch matcher waits for every file for day T. ACQ-TH1 delivers at 06:30 ICT (07:30 SGT) and ACQ-ID1 at 05:00 WIB (06:00 SGT). Matching takes 45 minutes and report generation a further 15 minutes at 2025 volume. Reports therefore finish around 08:30 SGT at best, and later at the roughly doubled 2027 volume. NFR-8 requires publication by 08:00 SGT on T+1. There is also no defined behaviour when a file is late or missing, which would block all merchants' reports.

Section 11.1 classes 'no response within 2,500 ms' as retryable, and Section 11.2 discards late responses. Yet Section 11.2 says cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the previous attempt 'did not succeed'. A timed-out attempt may still have been approved by the first acquirer, and the second acquirer may then approve too, leaving two holds on the customer's card. The design has no path to reverse or void an orphaned late approval, which conflicts with P1 and with the intent of FR-5 and FR-7.

Section 28 puts first-cohort go-live after Phase 7. The Fraud Hook comes in Phase 8 (blocked on the FRV-1 contract), and the load, DR, PCI DSS assessment and Section 26 acceptance testing come in Phase 9. Live card traffic would therefore run without the fraud scoring that FR-9 requires and before NFR-5 and the acceptance criteria have been demonstrated. Section 27's conclusion that only the Admin API and disputes are material gaps for the first cohort overlooks this.

Section 18.4 lets one Finance or Owner user change the payout account. The only notice goes to the user who made the change. MFA is enforced only for the Owner role. One phished Finance password is therefore enough to redirect all of a merchant's payouts: an account-takeover path to direct financial loss. Finance also holds both refund and payout-account rights, which conflicts with P9's separation of money-moving and configuration permissions.

Section 9.3 assumes a single partition sustains 10,000 WCU per second and that one merchant's roughly 1,800 writes per second fit comfortably. It also uses an LSI, which ties all of a merchant's items to one partition key. Both are external platform facts that the document does not support. It also counts writes rather than WCU for response bodies of up to 4 KB. If the per-partition limit or the LSI item-collection limits are lower than assumed, the durable idempotency path for M-0001 would throttle at campaign peak. That would break FR-5 and NFR-1 for 45% of peak traffic.

Section 7.2 permits PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED only, so a second partial refund, which FR-1 and FR-15 require, has no permitted transition. A payment refunded before settlement can never reach SETTLED, although Section 16.2 moves matched payments to SETTLED. Other paths have no clear transition: a failed 3DS challenge or wallet payment from REQUIRES_ACTION, the Section 8 REVIEW 'authorize-and-hold-capture' outcome, and repeated partial captures. The FR-2 property test only checks that no transition outside Section 7.2 occurs, so it cannot reveal missing transitions.

FR-5 requires the identical response even for concurrent duplicates, while Section 9.1 returns HTTP 409 request_in_progress to an in-flight duplicate. The FR-5 acceptance test resends only after the first response has arrived. It therefore never exercises the concurrent case, the sweeper-recovered IN_PROGRESS case, or the Redis-down path in Section 20.4, which are where duplicate downstream authorizations would arise.

Section 24 confirms network tokens as the primary card-on-file credential from launch, and Phase 3 (including card-on-file with network tokens) is marked 'No - ready'. Backlog item 2 says the VTS/MDES token-requestor application, the TSP agreement and certification have not started. The review adds two points. First, scheme registration and certification lead times sit on the critical path to first go-live, yet the readiness assessment does not track them. Second, the FR-14 test needs live network-token-enabled test cards, which depend on that registration.

Section 11 cascades issuer responses such as 05 'do not honour' to a different acquirer and says it stops 'at the scheme limits applicable to the card'. However, it does not state those limits or whether the schemes treat re-presenting an issuer decline through another acquirer as a reattempt or as a breach of their rules. The 31% recovery figure comes from a single-corridor pilot (ACQ-SG1 to ACQ-SG2) and is not split between issuer declines and acquirer errors. If scheme rules are stricter, FR-7 exposes merchants to excessive-reattempt fees, and the recovery benefit is unproven.

All primary data for five markets sits in Singapore, DR is in Jakarta, and card numbers plus hashed identifiers go to FRV-1 for a regional consortium graph. NFR-7 names each market's law but the design gives no transfer basis, localisation assessment (notably for Indonesian payment data) or vendor-sharing assessment. The FRV-1 DPA is acknowledged as pending in Backlog item 4. This review adds that the gap is wider than the vendor contract: the data-placement decision itself needs a per-market sign-off before build, not only the DPO review in Phase 9.

FR-8 caps the loss of authorization rate at 'more than 2%'. Section 10.3 and the confirmed Routing decision use a tolerance of 'default 2' with no unit. This could mean 2 percentage points or 2% relative, and either a per-transaction comparison of priors or a weekly realised-rate check. The weighted score in Section 10.2 can also choose a cheaper acquirer whatever the tolerance. With a default weighting that favours cost, the readings lead to materially different routing, and the FR-8 test cannot confirm the requirement.

Section 27 marks the Idempotency Layer and the Card Vault 'Ready', and concludes that the transaction core is specified to implementation level. Yet this review found principle and requirement conflicts in exactly those components: fast-path scoping (FND-001), Fraud Hook PAN access (FND-002), CVC retention (FND-003), HSM topology (FND-006) and the network-token dependency (FND-010). Section 27 is the document's own fitness verdict, so overstating it means build starts on parts that will need redesign.

The finding's main premises hold against §7.2. REQUIRES_ACTION can only move to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED (expiry). A failed 3DS challenge, or a wallet or bank payment that the provider reports as failed, therefore has no permitted path to FAILED, even though §8 says the provider notification drives the final transition and §11.4 says a failure returns FAILED. CAPTURED and SUCCEEDED can go to PARTIALLY_REFUNDED, but PARTIALLY_REFUNDED can only go to REFUNDED, never to SETTLED. A payment refunded before its settlement line is matched therefore cannot take the SETTLED transition that §16.2 requires. That matters elsewhere too: §12.4 deletes the CVC on SETTLED, though the 72-hour cap still applies. The FR-2 test in §26.1 only checks for disallowed transitions, so it cannot catch missing ones. Two points are weaker: repeated partial refunds and repeated partial captures could be read as self-loops. Even so, the finding is specific, grounded in the document, not in the answer key and not covered by any other finding.

FND-001.premise: Section 9.2 keys the Redis fast-path cache on idem:resp:{idempotency_key} alone, with no merchant_id. A cache hit returns the stored response straight away, without comparing request hashes. This conflicts with P3's (merchant, key) scoping, and Section 9.1 explicitly accepts merchants' own order and invoice IDs as keys.
FND-001.label: SUPPORTED
FND-001.doc_passage: On completion of a request, the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL. On every incoming mutating request, the Payments API checks this key first; on a hit, it returns the stored response immediately without touching DynamoDB or the Orchestrator.
FND-001.rationale: The document backs every factual claim in the finding. In Section 9.2, the fast-path key contains only the idempotency key, with no merchant identity. A cache hit returns the stored response without going to DynamoDB, and DynamoDB is the only place the request_hash comparison happens. So the fast path never checks the body hash. P3 says idempotency is scoped to (merchant, key). Section 9.1 says merchants often use their own order or invoice IDs as keys and that this is accepted. FR-5 requires a 422 when a key is reused with a different body. Section 24 repeats the key format "idem:resp:{key}".

FND-002.premise: Section 13.1 says the Fraud Hook detokenises the full PAN, using the Card Adapter's client library and service role, and sends it to FRV-1. This conflicts with P2 (PAN leaves the Vault only over the Card Adapter's acquirer connection), with Section 12.1 (only the Card Adapter's identity may detokenise) and with Section 12.2 (Fraud Hook is out of CDE scope and handles token, BIN and last 4 only). The FRV-1 data processing agreement is still pending as Backlog item 4.
FND-002.label: SUPPORTED
FND-002.doc_passage: card_number Vault detokenise Cross-merchant velocity graph ... FRV-1's consortium velocity graph is keyed on the full card number ... The Fraud Hook obtains the PAN through the Vault's detokenise operation, using the Card Adapter client library and service role.
FND-002.rationale: The document says what the finding claims. Section 13.1 lists card_number, obtained via Vault detokenise, in the FRV-1 payload, and says the Fraud Hook uses the Card Adapter's client library and service role to get it. P2 says PAN never leaves the Vault boundary except over the Card Adapter's connection to an acquirer. Section 12.1 says "Only the Card Adapter's service identity may call detokenise." Section 12.2 lists the Fraud Hook as "Out of scope — Token, BIN, last 4 only." Backlog item 4 confirms the FRV-1 data processing agreement is pending. The finding paraphrases Section 12.2 slightly, dropping "last 4", but this doesn't change its meaning.

FND-004.premise: NFR-4 requires zero RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings even if a whole region is lost, but Section 20.2 uses asynchronous Aurora Global replication with typical lag under one second and rebuilds DynamoDB, Redis and MSK empty after failover, and the NFR-4 game day only checks postings committed before the failure.
FND-004.label: SUPPORTED
FND-004.doc_passage: Aurora Global Database replicates the payments and ledger cluster to ap-southeast-3. Replication is storage-level and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second. • MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache are not replicated cross-region; on regional failover they are recreated empty in ap-southeast-3 from infrastructure-as-code, and in-flight idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table.
FND-004.rationale: The document backs each part of the finding's premise. NFR-4 says: "Recovery point objective for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region." Section 20.2 says Aurora Global Database replication is asynchronous, with typical lag under one second. It also says MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache are not replicated across regions and are recreated empty in ap-southeast-3. The NFR-4 acceptance test in Section 26.2 checks only that "every ledger posting committed in ap-southeast-1 before the failure is present after failover." Two parts of the finding go beyond the document's text. One is that idempotency state "cannot be fully rebuilt," which conflicts with the document's statement that it is reconstructed from the payment table. The other is that this would lead to duplicate authorizations. Both are inferences about consequences, not claims about what the document says.

FND-029.premise: Section 12.4 keeps the CVC encrypted in the Vault until settlement or for up to 72 hours, reuses it for cascade re-presentations and incremental authorizations, and justifies this by saying PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow SAD to be kept in encrypted form until the transaction is settled. NFR-6 cites the same requirements.
FND-029.label: SUPPORTED
FND-029.doc_passage: The CVC is required for the initial customer-initiated authorization and, at several acquirers, for each re-presentation of the credential during a cascade and for incremental authorizations (ride-hailing tips, hotel extensions). The Vault therefore stores the CVC encrypted under a separate KEK, and deletes it when the Reconciliation Service marks the associated payment SETTLED, or after 72 hours, whichever is first. This is permitted by PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2, which allow sensitive authentication data to be retained in encrypted form until the transaction is settled.
FND-029.rationale: The document says what the finding claims. Section 12.4 stores the CVC encrypted until settlement or for 72 hours, whichever comes first. It reuses the CVC for cascades and incremental authorizations, and it cites PCI DSS 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 as allowing SAD retention until settlement. NFR-6 refers to the same requirements, and Section 11.2 confirms the CVC is pulled from the Vault for cascades. Whether the standard actually allows this is an external question and outside the premise check.

FND-006.premise: The document runs the Vault's KEKs on a single CloudHSM in ap-southeast-1a and unwraps every DEK in the HSM without caching. Its trigger for adding a second HSM is sustained card volume above 1,500 TPS, but peak card volume is about 1,100 TPS (55% of 2,000). It also sets a 99.95% availability target and confirms "one HSM at launch".
FND-006.label: SUPPORTED
FND-006.doc_passage: The Vault's KEKs are held in an AWS CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. CloudHSM takes automatic daily backups of the cluster to S3, from which a new HSM can be created in any AZ. A second HSM will be added to the cluster when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. If the HSM is unreachable, the Vault returns HTTP 503 and the Card Adapter maps this to a retryable outcome.
FND-006.rationale:
The document backs up each factual claim in the finding:
- **Single HSM:** Section 12.3 states one HSM in ap-southeast-1a and a 1,500 TPS trigger for adding a second.
- **No DEK caching:** Section 12.1 says each detokenise call unwraps the DEK inside the HSM and DEKs are not cached.
- **Same Vault on every cascade:** Section 11.2 says each cascade attempt has the Card Adapter retrieve the credential from the Vault.
- **Card volume:** Section 1 puts the 2027 card share at 55% and peak at 2,000 TPS. That gives about 1,100 card TPS, below the 1,500 trigger.
- **Availability target:** NFR-3 sets 99.95%.
- **Approved decision:** Section 24 confirms "one HSM at launch".

FND-016.premise: The document treats a 2,500 ms acquirer timeout as retryable and cascades to the next acquirer. It discards late responses, yet claims cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the previous attempt did not succeed, and it defines no way to reverse or void a late approval that ends up orphaned.
FND-016.label: SUPPORTED
FND-016.doc_passage: Because each attempt carries its own attempt_id and the previous attempt did not succeed, cascading cannot create a duplicate charge: the ledger records only the approved attempt. Responses that arrive for an attempt after its 2,500 ms timeout are logged against the attempt and discarded.
FND-016.rationale: The document says what the finding claims. Section 11.1 lists "no response within 2,500 ms" as Retryable, with the action "Cascade to next candidate". Section 11.2 says late responses are logged and discarded, and it claims cascading cannot create a duplicate charge. I searched the whole document for any reversal or void of a late-approved attempt and found none. The stuck-payment sweeper (20.3) only resolves payments that are still AUTHORISING. The expiry sweeper (Section 7) voids uncaptured authorizations at the payment level, one day before scheme expiry. It does not void orphaned approvals on attempts that were superseded by a cascade. So the absence claim holds.

FND-005.premise: Section 21.1 leaves cascades out of the p99 on the grounds that fewer than 1% of card payments cascade, but Section 10.5 reports 3.8% retryable outcomes, Section 11.2 cascades every retryable outcome (including after a 2,500 ms timeout), and NFR-2 and its acceptance test both include cascades with 3.8% retryable injection.
FND-005.label: SUPPORTED
FND-005.doc_passage: Cascading does not move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade; the cascade path therefore sits above the 99th percentile. [§21.1] / retryable outcomes - soft declines eligible for reattempt plus acquirer-side errors and timeouts - 3.8%. [§10.5] / On a retryable outcome, the Retry Engine immediately submits a new attempt, with a new attempt_id, to the next acquirer in the Routing Engine's candidate list. [§11.2]
FND-005.rationale: The finding's premise matches the document. Section 21.1 says fewer than 1% of card payments cascade. Section 10.5 gives 3.8% retryable outcomes, and Section 11.2 cascades immediately on any retryable outcome. Section 11.1 counts "no response within 2,500 ms" as retryable, so a timeout-triggered cascade by itself takes longer than 1,500 ms. NFR-2 says "including any cascade," and the NFR-2 acceptance test uses "3.8% retryable-outcome injection." The scheme reattempt limits in Section 11.3 could stop a few retries, but nothing in the document cuts the cascade share from 3.8% to under 1%.

FND-020.premise: The document says the batch matcher waits for every file for day T. The latest file is ACQ-TH1's at 06:30 ICT (07:30 SGT). Matching takes 45 minutes and report generation another 15 minutes at 2025 volume. Reports would therefore finish around 08:30 SGT, which misses NFR-8's 08:00 SGT deadline, and the document defines no behaviour for late or missing files.
FND-020.label: SUPPORTED
FND-020.doc_passage: The batch matcher starts once all expected files for business day T have been received ... At 2025 volume, the matcher's measured end-to-end run time is 45 minutes, and merchant settlement report generation takes a further 15 minutes. [16.1: ACQ-TH1 CSV over SFTP Daily 06:30 ICT] [NFR-8: merchant settlement reports for business day T shall be published by 08:00 SGT on T+1.]
FND-020.rationale: The document backs the finding. Section 16.2 says matching waits for all files, and gives 45 minutes for matching plus 15 for report generation. Section 16.1 lists ACQ-TH1 at 06:30 ICT. ICT is UTC+7 and SGT is UTC+8, so that is 07:30 SGT. All other files arrive earlier: ACQ-ID1 at 06:00 SGT, and the sponsor banks by 05:00 SGT at the latest. Starting at 07:30 SGT and adding 60 minutes gives about 08:30 SGT, later than NFR-8's 08:00 SGT deadline. I also found no section that says what happens when a file is late or missing.

FND-021.premise: Section 28 schedules first-cohort go-live after Phase 7, but the Fraud Hook is built in Phase 8 (blocked on the FRV-1 contract) and the PCI DSS assessment and Section 26 test plan come in Phase 9, while Section 27 names only the Admin API schemas and disputes as material gaps.
FND-021.label: SUPPORTED
FND-021.doc_passage: 8 Fraud Hook (FRV-1) Yes - vendor contract (Backlog item 4) / 9 Hardening - load, chaos and DR game days; PCI DSS assessment; Section 26 test plan Follows Section 26 / The first merchant cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) goes live after Phase 7; other markets follow at four-week intervals.
FND-021.rationale: The document backs every factual part of the finding. Section 28 lists the Fraud Hook as Phase 8, blocked on the vendor contract (Backlog item 4). It lists load and DR game days, the PCI DSS assessment and the Section 26 test plan as Phase 9. It says the first cohort, which includes cards, goes live after Phase 7. FR-9 requires every card payment to be fraud-scored before authorization. Section 27's overall conclusion names only the Admin API schemas and the dispute module as material gaps and says neither blocks the first cohort.

FND-046.premise: Section 18.4 lets a single Finance or Owner user change the payout bank account with no second approval, and only the user who made the change gets a confirmation email. MFA is enforced only for the Owner role, and the Finance role holds both refund and payout-account-edit permissions.
FND-046.label: SUPPORTED
FND-046.doc_passage: A Finance or Owner user can change the payout bank account in the portal. The change takes effect from the next payout cycle. A confirmation email is sent to the user who made the change, and the change is written to the audit log.
FND-046.rationale: Section 18.4 matches the finding: one Finance or Owner user can make the change, and the confirmation email goes only to that user. It mentions no second approver and no alert to the Owner. Section 18.3 enforces TOTP only for the Owner role and leaves it optional for other roles. In 18.2, the Finance role has both "Issue refunds" and "edit payout bank account". P9 states that money-moving permissions are separated from configuration permissions. So every factual claim about the document holds.

FND-009.premise: Section 9.3 says a single DynamoDB partition sustains 10,000 WCU/s and that M-0001's roughly 1,800 writes/s fit within it. It counts each write as one WCU even though response bodies can be up to 4 KB. It also uses an LSI keyed on merchant_id, which puts all of a merchant's items under one partition key.
FND-009.label: SUPPORTED
FND-009.doc_passage: DynamoDB serves each partition key value from a single partition, and a single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units per second. Our largest merchant (marketplace M-0001) peaks at approximately 900 create-payment TPS during campaign events (45% of 2,000 TPS). Each request consumes two writes - lock acquisition and completion update - or about 1,800 WCU at peak, comfortably within the perpartition ceiling. Keying by merchant_id keeps each merchant's records co-located, which the local secondary index on created_at uses to serve the back-office "recent requests by merchant" view without a scan.
FND-009.rationale: Section 9.3 states the 10,000 WCU per-partition figure without citing anything to back it. It treats each of the two writes per request as one WCU ("about 1,800 WCU"), even though the table definition lists response_body as "up to 4 KB". It keys the table by merchant_id and uses an LSI on created_at. Nowhere does the document discuss WCU sizing by item size or LSI item-collection size limits. So what the finding says about the document is accurate.

FND-022.premise: Section 7.2's list of permitted transitions has no transition for a second partial refund (PARTIALLY_REFUNDED to PARTIALLY_REFUNDED), from a refunded state to SETTLED, from REQUIRES_ACTION to FAILED, or for repeated partial captures, and the FR-2 test only checks that no transition outside Section 7.2 occurs.
FND-022.label: SUPPORTED
FND-022.doc_passage:
CREATED -> REQUIRES_ACTION | AUTHORISING | FAILED | CANCELLED
REQUIRES_ACTION -> AUTHORISING | CANCELLED (expiry)
AUTHORISING -> AUTHORISED | SUCCEEDED | FAILED
AUTHORISED -> CAPTURED | CANCELLED (void or auth expiry)
CAPTURED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
SUCCEEDED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
SETTLED -> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED
FND-022.rationale:
The finding's claims about the document check out:
- **Second partial refund:** Section 7.2 lists only PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED. There is no self-transition, so a second partial refund has no permitted transition.
- **Refunded before settlement:** Neither PARTIALLY_REFUNDED nor REFUNDED can move to SETTLED. Yet Section 16.2 says "Matched payments transition to SETTLED."
- **Failed 3DS or wallet payment:** REQUIRES_ACTION can only go to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED (expiry). There is no direct path to FAILED.
- **Repeated partial captures:** There is no CAPTURED -> CAPTURED transition.
- **FR-2 test:** The Section 26.1 criterion only checks that sequences "never produce a transition outside Section 7.2" and that acknowledged transitions are saved. It does not check whether needed transitions are missing.

One point is debatable: the REVIEW "authorize-and-hold-capture" outcome could arguably use AUTHORISED. The finding only says that path lacks a clear transition, which is consistent with the text.

FND-023.premise: FR-5 requires the identical response even for concurrent duplicate requests, while Section 9.1 returns HTTP 409 to an in-flight duplicate, and the FR-5 acceptance test only resends after the first response is received, so it never tests the concurrent case.
FND-023.label: SUPPORTED
FND-023.doc_passage: FR-5: "...shall return the identical response, including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently." §9.1: "While the first request is in flight, a duplicate receives HTTP 409 request_in_progress with Retry-After: 1." §26.1 FR-5: "Send a create-payment request; after its response is received, resend the identical request with the same Idempotency-Key. The second response is byte-identical to the first and the acquirer simulator records exactly one authorization. Resending with a modified body returns 422."
FND-023.rationale: The finding quotes all three passages correctly. FR-5 requires an identical response for concurrent duplicates. Section 9.1 says an in-flight duplicate gets a 409, which is not the same response. The Section 26.1 test resends only after the first response has come back, so it is sequential. No other FR-5 test covers concurrent duplicates, the sweeper-recovered IN_PROGRESS case, or the Redis-down path.

FND-036.premise: The document commits to network tokens as the primary card-on-file credential from launch and marks Phase 3 (card-on-file with network tokens) as 'No - ready', yet Backlog item 2 says the VTS/MDES token-requestor application, TSP agreement and certification are outstanding, and the readiness assessment does not track this dependency.
FND-036.label: SUPPORTED
FND-036.doc_passage: Token Requestor onboarding - Visa VTS and Mastercard MDES token-requestor registration (TRID) and the commercial agreement with a token service provider; certification test plan. Application not yet submitted.
FND-036.rationale: The finding's claims about the document all check out. Section 24 says "Network tokens (VTS/MDES) as the primary credential for all card-on-file and recurring payments from launch". Section 28, Phase 3, covers "card-on-file with network tokens" and is marked "No - ready". Backlog item 2 lists TRID registration, the TSP agreement and the certification test plan as not fully designed, with "Application not yet submitted." Section 27 rates the Card Vault and Card Adapter "Ready" and says network tokens are "specified", without pointing to Backlog item 2. So the readiness assessment does not track this dependency. The FR-14 acceptance test does call for a "network-token-enabled test card".

FND-039.premise: Section 11 cascades issuer soft declines such as 05 to another acquirer and says it stops 'at the scheme limits applicable to the card', but never states those limits or whether cross-acquirer re-presentment of an issuer decline counts as a reattempt; the 31% recovery figure comes from a single ACQ-SG1→ACQ-SG2 pilot and is not split between issuer declines and acquirer errors.
FND-039.label: SUPPORTED
FND-039.doc_passage: The Retry Engine maintains a per-card (PAN fingerprint) and per-merchant reattempt counter over a rolling 30-day window and stops reattempting at the scheme limits applicable to the card. Responses carrying "do not reattempt" advice are classed as Final regardless of response code.
FND-039.rationale: Section 11.1 lists 05, 91 and 96 as retryable soft declines that cascade to the next acquirer. Section 11.3 mentions "the scheme limits applicable to the card" but never gives the actual limit values. I found no section, including Sections 24 and 26 (FR-7 says only "stop at scheme reattempt limits"), that gives numeric limits or says whether sending an issuer decline through a different acquirer counts as a reattempt. Section 10.5 confirms that the 31% figure comes from one three-month ACQ-SG1 → ACQ-SG2 pilot. It reports that figure for all retryable outcomes combined, with no split between issuer soft declines and acquirer errors.

FND-051.premise: The design places all primary data for the five markets in Singapore, keeps DR in Jakarta, and sends card numbers and hashed identifiers to FRV-1, but it gives no cross-border transfer basis, no data-localisation assessment (for example for Indonesian payment data) and no vendor-sharing assessment beyond naming each market's law in NFR-7 and listing the pending FRV-1 DPA.
FND-051.label: SUPPORTED
FND-051.doc_passage: All primary data stores (Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, MSK, S3 intake and archive buckets) are in ap-southeast-1. The Aurora Global Database secondary in ap-southeast-3 (Jakarta) is used for disaster recovery only (Section 20).
FND-051.rationale: The finding's factual claims all check out. Section 19.1 puts all primary data in ap-southeast-1 and the DR copy in Jakarta. Section 13.1 sends card_number plus SHA-256 email and phone to FRV-1's regional consortium graph. NFR-7 only names each market's law and lists purpose limitation, retention and access logging. Backlog item 4 lists the FRV-1 DPA as pending. NFR-7 is checked only by a DPO sign-off in Section 26, which runs in Phase 9. I searched the whole document for a cross-border transfer basis, a localisation or data-residency assessment, and an assessment of sharing data with the vendor, including under other wording, and found none.

FND-012.premise: Section 27 rates the Idempotency Layer and the Card Vault/Card Adapter as 'Ready' and concludes that the transaction core is specified to implementation level.
FND-012.label: SUPPORTED
FND-012.doc_passage: Idempotency Layer Ready Two-tier design, key schema and capacity specified (Section 9). ... Card Vault and Card Adapter Ready Tokenisation, envelope encryption, HSM, SAD handling and network tokens specified (Section 12). ... The transaction core is specified to implementation level. The Admin API schemas and the dispute module are the two material gaps
FND-012.rationale: The finding says the document claims these components are ready, and Section 27 does make that claim. Its table rates both the Idempotency Layer and the Card Vault/Card Adapter as 'Ready'. Its overall conclusion says the transaction core is specified to implementation level and names only the Admin API schemas and the dispute module as material gaps. The quoted text matches the document. Whether the underlying conflicts are real is a matter for the other findings this one cites (FND-001, -002, -003, -006 and -010), not part of this premise.

FND-011.premise: FR-8 states a "more than 2%" authorization-rate cap, but Section 10.3 and the Section 24 Routing decision give the tolerance only as "default 2" with no unit. The document never says whether this means percentage points or a relative 2%. It also describes two different mechanisms: a per-transaction comparison of priors and a weekly check of realised rates.
FND-011.label: SUPPORTED
FND-011.doc_passage: At routing time, the engine compares the approval prior of the lowest-cost acquirer against that of the highest-approval acquirer and applies the cost preference when the difference is within the configured tolerance (default 2). Separately, the weekly Routing Review compares each merchant's realised authorization rate under cost-preferred routing against a control slice (5% of traffic routed approval-first) and adjusts weights where the merchant's authorization rate has fallen by more than the tolerance.
FND-011.rationale: FR-8 says "by more than 2%". Section 10.3 says "within the configured tolerance (default 2)", and Section 24 says "cost-preferred within 2 tolerance". Neither gives a unit. I searched the whole document for "percentage points", "relative" and similar wording and found nothing that defines the unit. Section 10.3 does describe both a per-transaction prior comparison and a separate weekly realised-rate review. Section 10.2 has a weighted score whose default "emphasises cost". The finding's description of the document is accurate.
